title: ADAlign: Automatic Graph Alignment Without Manual Rules
one_liner: Instead of hand-coding which parts of a graph to align when transferring between different graph datasets, this method learns automatically what to align for each new task.
lead: When you train a machine learning model on one graph (a network of connected things like social networks or molecules) and then apply it to a different graph, the patterns can be very different. Most methods ask you to guess which parts matter — connections? Node labels? Both? This paper introduces a system that automatically figures out what to align for each transfer task, without you having to guess.

problem.h2: Hand-coded rules break across different transfer tasks
paras: When you train a model on one graph and move it to a different graph, the two graphs are rarely identical. The node labels (like user age or product category) might differ, the connection patterns might differ, or both.

Existing methods force you to choose upfront: align the node labels? Align the connection structure? Design a specific filter for this pair of graphs? Each choice requires guessing which parts of the two graphs matter most, and that guess changes depending on what transfer task you are doing. A rule that works perfectly when moving from social-network-A to social-network-B fails when moving from social-network-A to molecule-B, because the relevant patterns shifted.

callout.html: When moving a trained model to a new graph, you must manually specify which graph features to align, but the right choice depends on the task and changes unpredictably.

steps.text: Convert each graph into a mathematical form using spectral methods.
Score which spectral components (frequency bands) show the biggest mismatch.
Emphasize the spectral bands where source and target differ most.
Bring source and target into agreement on those key components automatically.
Model now works better on target because patterns are aligned.

paras: The paper changes how you decide which parts of a graph to align. Instead of writing down a fixed rule (align attributes, or align structure, or both in a preset way), the method learns which alignment target to pick by scoring the spectral components (frequency bands) of each graph and finding which ones differ most.

hidden.name: spectral mismatch score
paras: A spectral mismatch score measures how different two graphs are at each frequency band. A graph has different signal strength at different frequencies, just as radio signals vary across the dial. The method compares source and target graphs on each frequency band and finds where they disagree most.

The paper measures this using a neural characteristic function, a mathematical tool that encodes all the ways the two graphs' node labels and connection patterns interact, across all orders and scales. Instead of manually picking which interaction order matters, the method learns which spectral bands (frequencies) matter most for this specific task, and emphasizes those when aligning.

heat.caption: Darker means bigger mismatch between source and target at that frequency band. Boxes mark bands the method adaptively emphasizes.

reads.html: The method finds the radio frequencies where source and target graphs sound most different, then focuses on making them sound the same at those frequencies.
Neural Spectral Discrepancy uses a learnable frequency sampler in the spectral domain to adaptively identify and emphasize informative cross-graph discrepancies through a minimax objective.

paras: A graph is fundamentally a set of numbers (node labels, connection strengths) arranged in a specific pattern. The spectral view decomposes that pattern into frequency bands, from global slow changes to sharp local detail. When you move a trained model from one graph to another, the model has learned to respond to certain frequencies in the source graph. If the target graph has different power at those frequencies, the model's predictions will be wrong.

By automatically identifying which frequencies matter most (where the mismatch is biggest) and aligning those, the method ensures the target graph's frequency signature matches the source. The model then sees a familiar pattern and works correctly. Rather than manually picking whether to align labels or structure, the right features to align are determined by which ones differ most between source and target.

math.words: The Neural Spectral Discrepancy measures the weighted sum of differences at each frequency, where weights are learned to emphasize the most informative frequencies for the task.

worked.title: A tiny worked example with three frequency bands
lines: Frequency 1: source=8, target=5, distance=3, learned weight=0.8 -> penalty: 0.8 * 3 = 2.4
Frequency 2: source=4, target=6, distance=2, learned weight=0.2 -> penalty: 0.2 * 2 = 0.4
Frequency 3: source=7, target=7, distance=0, learned weight=0.5 -> penalty: 0.5 * 0 = 0.0
Total NSD = 2.4 + 0.4 + 0.0 = 2.8. The method learned that frequency 1 matters most (weight 0.8) and frequency 2 matters least (0.2), so it focused the alignment effort there.

math.note: The weights (one per frequency) are not fixed upfront; they are learned during training to identify which frequencies are most informative for the specific transfer task, making the alignment adaptive.

charts.title: Hand-coded rule (fixed alignment)
charts.note: A fixed alignment rule ignores which features actually matter for this specific transfer task.

charts.title: Adaptive alignment (ADAlign)
charts.note: Automatic discovery of important frequencies works better because the method focuses alignment effort on the frequencies that actually matter for this specific transfer task. The model learns by recognizing patterns in data; when those patterns match between source and target at the frequencies the model uses most, the model's knowledge transfers directly without requiring extensive retraining.

items.b: Source and target are too different.
items.html: If the two graphs are fundamentally different (a social network and a molecule database), even aligning every frequency may not be enough, because the task itself may be unsolvable with source knowledge.

items.b: The learned weights overfit to the training split.
items.html: If the method learns which frequencies matter by only observing the source and target in one transfer scenario, those weights may not generalize to new transfer tasks with different frequency importance.

The spectral view works best when the graph patterns vary smoothly across frequencies. If patterns are highly chaotic or have sharp anomalies, the frequency decomposition may not capture the important structure.
Validate the learned weights on held-out transfer scenarios and retrain if needed. Use spectral alignment as a preprocessing step, not the only adaptation method.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple demo with two small synthetic graphs (e.g. two random networks with different connection densities and node label distributions). Train a classifier on the source graph. Run three transfer methods: (1) no alignment, (2) hand-coded alignment (always align node labels), (3) ADAlign. For each, measure accuracy on the target graph. ADAlign should automatically discover that node labels matter more than structure (or vice versa, depending on the synthetic data), and transfer more accurately than the hand-coded baseline even though it requires zero manual tuning.
demo.closing: The demo must show that learned weights discover the right alignment targets automatically, without any manual rule design for this specific transfer scenario.
